script.title: Why Lilienthal Built His Own Hill

lines: A German engineer built his own hill to launch his gliders from.
Otto Lilienthal and his brother Gustav studied the flight of birds.
Together they made strap-on wings, but failed to fly.
In 1891, Lilienthal made his first glider jumps from a sand pit on a hill.
In 1894, near his home in Lichterfelde, he built a cone-shaped hill, 15 metres high.
It allowed him to launch his gliders into the wind, no matter which direction it was coming from.
You see, it's like flying a kite.
You always turn to face the wind first.
A regular crowd came to watch him.
He made over 2,000 flights in gliders of his own design.
Reports and photographs of his flights spread, and he became known as the father of flight.
But his gliders tended to pitch down.
He held them by his shoulders, which limited how much he could shift his weight.
Lilienthal fell from about 15 metres and broke his neck.
In 1932, his hill, the Fliegeberg, was redesigned as a memorial to him.

claims.claim: Lilienthal studied the flight of birds with his brother Gustav; Lilienthal and his brother made strap-on wings, but failed in their attempts to fly.
In the spring of 1891, Lilienthal managed the first jumps and flights on the slope of a sand pit on a hill; in 1891 he succeeded with jumps and flights covering a distance of about 25 metres.

He built an artificial conical hill in 1894 near his home in Lichterfelde. It allowed him to launch his gliders into the wind no matter which direction it was coming from. The hill was 15 metres high.
There was a regular crowd of people that were interested in seeing his gliding experiments.
Lilienthal made over 2,000 flights in gliders of his design.
Reports of Lilienthal's flights spread in Germany and elsewhere, with photographs appearing in scientific and popular publications; he soon became known as the father of flight.
His gliders had a tendency to pitch down; he held the glider by his shoulders, and only his legs and lower body could be moved, which limited the amount of weight shift he could achieve.
On 9 August 1896, Lilienthal's glider stalled. Falling from about 15 metres, he broke his neck and died the next day.
The Fliegeberg was redesigned by a Berlin architect in 1932 as a memorial to Lilienthal.
